1.pericope_label: Appoint out for you cities of refuge: the manslayer and the congregation

schools.summary: Read the renewed command as a reproof. That it had not occurred to their own minds to designate the cities until they were again reminded indirectly censures their sluggishness, for the divine command had been given beyond the Jordan and the reason for it remained always equally valid: why then do they wait, and why do they not give full effect to what they had rightly begun? Hence we perceive how tardy men are, not only to perform their duty but to provide for their own safety, unless the Lord frequently urge them and prick them forward. Yet allow that they sinned only from thoughtlessness, since they are forthwith ready to obey, neither procrastinating nor creating obstacles to a necessary matter. On the institution itself, keep both sides in view: the asylum gave no impunity to voluntary murder, but if any one by mistake had slain a man with whom he was not at enmity he found a safe refuge; and respect was so far paid to the feelings of the brethren and kindred of the deceased that their sorrow was not increased by the constant presence of the man who had caused their bereavement. Note also that the people were accustomed by it to detest murder, since homicide even when not culpable brought exile from country and home until the death of the high priest — which clearly showed how precious human blood is in the sight of God. And observe at last that everything here is not mentioned in order, since one who had accidentally killed a man might have remained in safety by presenting himself before the court and obtaining an acquittal after due investigation.

Supply the legal background, since without it the institution looks arbitrary. Such a provision was essentially necessary wherever the patriarchal law of redemption and the avenging of blood was in force, for the nearest of kin had not only the right of redeeming a forfeited inheritance but authority to slay on the spot the person who had slain his relative; so a man might casually kill another against whom he had no ill-will and lose his life to the avenger though he had not forfeited it to the law. The privileged city gave him protection until the cause had been fully heard by the magistrates, who had authority to deliver him up if on examination he was found not entitled to it. Then insist on the limit of the mercy. The word unwittingly is twice repeated, and the repetition cuts off all the expectations wilful murderers might have of protection here, God having declared that such should be taken even from his altar that they might be killed; from which turn on the present age — it is strange that any Christians should make their sanctuaries give protection to persons whom God has so expressly excepted from it. On the procedure, note that the gate is where the judges used to sit, that declaring his cause means giving a true relation of the fact and all its circumstances, and that the congregation before which he must stand is not the council of the city of refuge, which had examined him already, but of the city to which he belonged or near which the fact was committed.

Take the appointment as timely rather than late: the land was newly surveyed, so they were the better able to divide its coasts into three parts for the more convenient situation of these cities; though it is probable the thing was not done till after the Levites had their portion assigned them in the next chapter, because the cities of refuge were all to be Levites' cities. Read the whole as a privilege to all Israel, since no man could be sure but some time it might be his own case, and it was for the interest of the land that the blood of an innocent person, whose hand only was guilty and not his heart, should not be shed. Then press the type. As soon as ever God had given them cities of rest he bade them appoint cities of refuge, which intimates what God's spiritual Israel have in Christ and heaven, not only rest to repose themselves in but refuge to secure themselves in; and so much care would not have been taken over these cities, when the courts might simply have been authorised to acquit the manslayer as our own law does, unless they were designed to typify the relief the gospel provides for poor penitent sinners and their protection from the curse of the law. Finally, dwell on the accident itself: a man might kill his own child or dearest friend unawares, for the way of man is not in himself — and what reason have we to thank God who has kept us both from slaying and from being slain.

debates.question: Why were the cities of refuge not appointed before now?

sides.position: Their sluggishness is indirectly censured: the command was given beyond the Jordan and the reason for it remained always equally valid
The proper time had not arrived, since every city of refuge had to be Levitical and the Levites' portion was not assigned until the next chapter

debates.question: May a sanctuary shelter a wilful murderer?

sides.position: No, and the doubled word 'unwittingly' says so: such were to be taken even from God's altar, which condemns the Christian sanctuaries that shelter them
The asylum gave no impunity to voluntary murder; the magistrates had authority to deliver up anyone found not entitled to protection

outliers.note: Alone reads the renewed command as a reproof of Israel's delay rather than as a step taken at its proper time, and a note printed with his own text answers him, observing that he is somewhat singular in this and that other expositors hold the appointment could not precede the allocation of cities to the Levites.

Alone turns the doubled 'unwittingly' into a polemic against his own age, finding it strange that any Christians should make their sanctuaries protect persons whom God has so expressly excepted; and alone distinguishes the congregation that judges the case from the elders of the city of refuge who had examined him already.

Alone sets out the patriarchal law that makes the institution necessary, in which the nearest of kin held both the right of redeeming a forfeited inheritance and the authority to kill the slayer on the spot, so that a man who killed by accident might lose his life though he had not forfeited it to the law.

themes: The Lord also spake unto Joshua, saying,
Speak to the children of Israel, saying, Appoint out for you cities of refuge, whereof I spake unto you by the hand of Moses:
That the slayer that killeth any person unawares and unwittingly may flee thither: and they shall be your refuge from the avenger of blood.

And when he that doth flee unto one of those cities shall stand at the entering of the gate of the city, and shall declare his cause in the ears of the elders of that city, they shall take him into the city unto them, and give him a place, that he may dwell among them.
And if the avenger of blood pursue after him, then they shall not deliver the slayer up into his hand; because he smote his neighbour unwittingly, and hated him not beforetime.

And he shall dwell in that city, until he stand before the congregation for judgment, and until the death of the high priest that shall be in those days: then shall the slayer return, and come unto his own city, and unto his own house, unto the city from whence he fled.

7.pericope_label: The six cities named, for the stranger as for the children of Israel

schools.summary: Give the geography and the philology, and no typology at all. In the north, Kedesh in Galil on the mountains of Naphtali — Galil meaning a circle, and the district called the circle of the heathen because an unusually large number of Gentiles were living there; in the centre, Shechem upon the mountains of Ephraim; in the south, Kirjath-arba, that is Hebron, upon the mountains of Judah. Beyond Jordan the three had already been appointed by Moses and are mentioned here again only for the sake of completeness. On the term used of them in the eighth verse, reject two standing renderings by name: it signifies neither cities of congregation nor cities of asylum, but cities of appointment — those which received the appointment already given and repeated in what follows.

Read the verb of appointment toward use rather than holiness: the Hebrew word here signifies also to fit and consecrate, so the cities were selected according as common use required, from which it is inferred that matters were well arranged so as to make private yield to public interest. Then notice what the arrangement cost, which nobody else does. Kirjath-Arbah, afterwards called Hebron, was transferred to the Levites though it had formerly been the property of Caleb; and in that appeared the rare, nay the incomparable moderation of this aged saint, who readily gave up to others both the city and its suburbs, which he had justly claimed as his right, the moment the lot showed that this was pleasing to God. It was necessary to advert to the change, because the Lord was pleased that asylums should be found only in the Levitical cities, so that innocence might be defended with greater fidelity and authority.

Explain why the cities were where they were: distributed through the land at proper distances so as to be convenient to every part, situated on eminences that they might be easily seen from afar, and the roads leading to them broad, even and always kept in good repair. Give the six names with their roots — Kedesh from a verb meaning to separate or set apart, and so holiness; Shechem from one meaning to be ready and diligent, hence the shoulder, ready to bear burdens, and by metaphor government; Hebron from a verb to associate or unite as friends, hence fellowship; Bezer from one meaning to enclose or encompass with a wall, hence a fortress — and then hand the matter over, giving each signification and leaving the application to others, with the remark that a person of the spirit and turn of Origen could preach the whole Gospel from these particulars. On the Levitical arrangement, note two reasons: that such causes might be more impartially examined by those best able to understand the law of God and least likely to be biassed by affection or corrupt interest, and that the reputation of the Levites with the people might restrain revengeful persons who followed the manslayer thither. And on the last verse, take the inclusion of the stranger as the point, since these typified the provision God was making for the salvation of both Jews and Gentiles, and the stranger had the same right to the benefit as the Israelite: is he the God of the Jews only?

Begin with the word: they are said to sanctify these cities, that being the original term for appointed. No ceremony was used to signify a consecration; they did but by a public act of court solemnly declare them cities of refuge, and as such sacred to the honour of God as the protector of exposed innocency — and if they were sanctuaries, it was proper to say they were sanctified. Note how they are placed: the three stood in the three several parts of the country so conveniently that a man might reach one of them in half a day from any corner, Kedesh in the most northern tribe, Hebron in the most southern, Shechem about equally distant from both; God is a refuge at hand. They stood on hills to be seen afar off, for a city on a hill cannot be hid, and though the poor man's way at last was up-hill, he would be in his place of safety quickly. And they were all Levites' cities, which put an honour upon God's tribe and was a kindness to the refugee, who when he might not go up to the house of the Lord nor tread his courts yet had the servants of God's house with him to instruct him and pray for him. On the names, say honestly that you delight not in quibbling upon names, and then take notice of them: Kedesh is holy, and our refuge is the holy Jesus; Shechem a shoulder, and the government is upon his shoulder; Hebron fellowship, into which believers are called; Bezer a fortification, for he is a strong-hold to them that trust in him; Ramoth high or exalted; Golan joy, for in him all the saints shall glory. Add one refuge the chapter does not name, the horns of the altar, which sheltered those who took hold of them where the crime was such as sanctuary allowed.

debates.question: Should the names of the six cities be read typologically?

sides.position: With a caveat: I delight not in quibbling upon names, yet am willing to take notice of these — Kedesh holy, Shechem a shoulder, Hebron fellowship
Give each signification and leave the application to others; a person of the spirit and turn of Origen could preach the whole Gospel from these particulars
Geography and philology only, with no application made

debates.question: What does the verb rendered 'appointed' at verse 7 mean?

sides.position: Sanctify: no ceremony was used, but a public act of court declared them sacred to the honour of God, and it was proper to say sanctuaries were sanctified
To fit and consecrate: the cities were selected according as common use required, private interest yielding to public

outliers.note: Alone notices what the arrangement cost an individual, that Kirjath-Arbah had been Caleb's own property before it passed to the Levites, and finds in his ready surrender of city and suburbs the moment the lot fell an incomparable moderation.

Alone rejects two standing renderings of the term used at verse 8 by naming the scholars who gave them, holding it means neither cities of congregation nor cities of asylum but cities of appointment; and alone explains that the district of Kedesh was called the circle of the heathen from the number of Gentiles living in it.

Alone gives a twofold reason for the cities being Levitical, that the judges would be least biassed by affection or corrupt interest and that their standing with the people would itself restrain a revengeful pursuer.

themes: And they appointed Kedesh in Galilee in mount Naphtali, and Shechem in mount Ephraim, and Kirjath–arba, which is Hebron, in the mountain of Judah.

And on the other side Jordan by Jericho eastward, they assigned Bezer in the wilderness upon the plain out of the tribe of Reuben, and Ramoth in Gilead out of the tribe of Gad, and Golan in Bashan out of the tribe of Manasseh.

These were the cities appointed for all the children of Israel, and for the stranger that sojourneth among them, that whosoever killeth any person at unawares might flee thither, and not die by the hand of the avenger of blood, until he stood before the congregation.
